Hi Priya,

We met at the SaaSBoomi session in Bengaluru on 3 September. You mentioned your SDRs lose about a day a week to bounced emails.

In June we rebuilt a 12,000-contact list for a Singapore fintech, and their bounce rate fell from 18% to 4% on the first send.

Would a 20-minute call on Thursday or Friday work to see if the same fix applies to your APAC list?

Deep
Three things changed in Q2: we added phone verification, we dropped two stale sources, and we moved refreshes from quarterly to monthly. Bounces fell 31% across 40,000 records.

The pilot did not include healthcare accounts, so the 4% bounce rate applies to fintech only. We have not tested the Japan segment yet, and we will share those numbers once the 900-record sample is back.
Your fridge is judging you. Restock it with Brik Oven sourdough and Araku coffee before dinner.
Cut openers like "Here's the thing" and words like "leverage" from client emails, and replace them with the fact you were about to state.

We missed the September target by 6 SQLs. Two of the misses came from the Japan list, which we sourced before the switch in August. We are re-verifying those 900 records this week and will send the revised count on Friday.

regression.text:
Most AI SDR pilots don't fail because of the AI.

In Q2, my team audited 3 AI SDR pilots at mid-market B2B companies. Each one had the same complaint: the agent was sending, but the replies weren't coming.

The problem wasn't the prompts, the sequences, or the model.

38% of the contacts the agents were emailing were stale. People who had left the company. Addresses that bounced.

The agents were doing exactly what they were told. They were just doing it to people who weren't there anymore.

So we re-verified the lists. Reply rates roughly doubled in all 3.

An AI SDR scales whatever you feed it. Give it a clean list and it scales conversations. Give it a stale one and it scales bounces, and leadership walks away convinced AI outbound doesn't work.

If you're about to launch a pilot, audit the list before you audit the agent.

What's the first thing your team checks before switching one on?

Why HCP contact data goes stale faster than you think

Your HCP database was accurate the day it was built. It probably isn't today.

Physicians change practice affiliation often. They join a new group, move to a hospital system, split time across clinics, or leave a practice altogether. Each move quietly breaks a record in your CRM. The name is still right. The specialty is still right. But the clinic your rep is driving to is one the physician no longer works at.

That's a cost most pharma marketing teams never see on a dashboard: a rep in the wrong waiting room, a visit that doesn't happen, a planned conversation that never takes place. Repeat that across a territory and a quarter, and stale affiliation data stops being a data problem. It becomes a field-force problem.

At Ampliz, we cover more than 4 million physicians and 9,000+ hospitals. Here's why HCP data decays so quickly, and what your team can do about it.

If your AI SDR pilot is stalling, check the list before you rewrite the prompts or the sequence. An agent will email a contact who has left the company as readily as one who is still in the job, and a bounce tells you nothing about whether your message worked.

When did your team last verify the contacts your agents are emailing?

Your rep drives to the clinic listed in your CRM, asks for the physician, and learns she now practices somewhere else. The visit is lost, and so is the rep's time.

Physicians change practice affiliation often. When a doctor moves to a new group or hospital, your records do not update on their own. The name and specialty still look right, so nobody flags the record. The affiliation is the part that went wrong, and it is the part that tells a rep where to go.

That makes affiliation the first field to check in any HCP list your team buys or maintains. A record can pass every other test and still send a rep to the wrong clinic.

Ampliz covers 4M+ physicians and 9,000+ hospitals. Across a physician base that size, frequent affiliation changes produce a steady stream of records that look correct and point to the wrong place.
